newsitem.title: USA: Apple reports $708 million second-quarter loss.
newsitem.headline: Apple reports $708 million second-quarter loss.

text.p: Apple Computer Inc. reported a second-quarter loss of $708 million Wednesday, reflecting one-time charges and weaker sales by the troubled computer maker.

Apple said the loss for the quarter ended March 28, which equalled $5.64 a share, compared with a loss of $740 million, or $5.99 a share, in the year-ago quarter, when Apple was also hit by one-time charges. Revenues fell to $1.6 billion in the latest quarter from $2.19 billion in last year's quarter.

The results included two previously announced one-time charges: $375 million for write-offs associated with the Feb. 4 acquisition of NeXT Software Inc. and $155 million to increase reserves to cover the costs of restructuring.

Excluding the charges, Apple posted an operating loss of $186 million, or $1.48 a share. That was slightly worse than the consensus industry analyst forecast of $1.22 a share, according to First Call, which tracks analysts' predictions.
But the Cupertino, Calif.-based company said it expected to see higher revenues and a reduced operating loss in the third quarter as its restructuring programme takes hold.

"We expect to see rapid improvements in the company's financial performance as the results of restructuring kick in," Apple Chief Financial Officer Fred Anderson said in a statement. "We anticipate higher revenues and a significantly reduced operating loss in the company's third fiscal quarter and continued progress toward our goal of returning to profitability in the fourth quarter."
Apple, which pioneered the personal computer, has struggled in recent years from missed opportunities, management turmoil and failed stratagies.

Over the last three years, the company has laid off thousands of workers and replaced most of its senior management. It fired former Chief Executive Michael Spindler last year, replacing him with outside board member Gilbert Amelio, and also hired back its two founders -- Steven Jobs and Stephen Wozniak -- to advise Amelio.

Aside from its other problems, Apple has been hurt by higher costs than its rivals because it needs to support both the hardware and software sides of its business. Other companies, such as software giant Microsoft Corp., can devote all of their financial resources to improving their software, while rival PC makers such as Compaq and Dell focus on the hardware.

Industry experts say Apple's ill-fated decision not to license the Macintosh operating system to other manufacturers kept the company's market share from growing and allowed rival Microsoft Corp. to dominate the industry with its Windows operating system.

By the time Apple reversed course, more than 80 percent of the world's computers were using Windows, making it difficult for Apple to make inroads even though many computer enthusiasts felt Apple's system was easier to use.
Compounding Apple's woes were a series of production and forecasting problems which prevented Apple from capitalising on the PC buying craze and the popularity of the Internet.
Dataquest, which tracks PC sales worldwide, says Apple's share of the worldwide market fell to 5.2 percent last year from 7.9 percent.
The slide left Apple's market share at the lowest point in three years.
